tool.name: HTTP & the web
tool.tagline: How browsers, servers and APIs talk: URLs, DNS, TLS, requests, caching and more
tool.description: HTTP is the protocol behind every web page and almost every API. This curriculum follows a request from URL and DNS lookup through TCP and TLS to methods, status codes, headers, caching, cookies and CORS, then on to REST design, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, real-time connections and CDNs. Understanding it makes you better at debugging, API design and web performance in any language.

glossary.def: One Name: value line of extra information at the top of an HTTP request or response, such as Content-Type: text/html.
Anything a URL points to on a server: a page, an image, a list of products, one customer's details.
The scheme, host and port of a URL together, like https://example.com:443. Browsers keep pages from different origins apart.
A small program you run in a terminal to send an HTTP request and print the response, e.g. curl -v https://example.com.
The HTTP method that asks for a response's headers only, without the body, e.g. to check that something exists or how big it is.
An HTTP method that promises not to change anything on the server: GET, HEAD and OPTIONS.
The DNS server your device asks to look up names; it finds the answer by asking other DNS servers and remembers it for a while.
In DNS, one stored entry for a name, such as its IP address (an A record), another name it points to (CNAME) or its mail server (MX).
The client says which formats or languages it prefers (Accept, Accept-Language headers) and the server picks the best version it has.
HTTP/1.1's way of sending a body in pieces as it's produced, when its total size isn't known in advance.
A cookie with no expiry date, deleted when the browser closes. (Login cookies are also loosely called session cookies.)
A cookie set by a different site than the one you're visiting, such as an ad network embedded in the page; most browsers now block or limit them.
The programming language that runs inside web pages in the browser; it can react to clicks, change the page and send requests.
A cache used by many people, such as a CDN or a company proxy, as opposed to a single user's browser cache.
A request that says "only send it if it changed", using If-None-Match or If-Modified-Since; the answer is 304 Not Modified if nothing changed.
A response header holding a version label for the content, like "v42"; caches send it back to ask whether the content changed.
A cache asking the server whether its stored copy is still current, instead of downloading it again.
The browser rule that a page's scripts may not read responses from a different origin unless that origin allows it (through CORS).
An automatic OPTIONS request a browser sends before certain cross-origin requests, asking the server whether the real request is allowed.
When one slow or lost item at the front of a queue holds up everything behind it, like one slow shopper at a single checkout.
Carrying many separate conversations over one connection at the same time, their pieces interleaved.
The header compression used by HTTP/2 (QPACK in HTTP/3); it avoids resending headers that repeat on every request.
Part of the TLS handshake where client and server agree which protocol to speak next, such as h2 (HTTP/2) or http/1.1.
A newer internet transport protocol built on UDP, with encryption built in and independent streams; HTTP/3 runs on it.
One of a CDN's many servers spread around the world, close to users, that answers requests from its cache or fetches from the origin server.
Your own server that a CDN or other cache fetches content from when it doesn't have a fresh copy.
A response header telling the browser to use only HTTPS for this site for a set time, even if someone types http://.
A response header listing where a page may load scripts, styles and other content from, limiting the damage of XSS.
A random value made fresh for one use, such as one response or one message, so it can't be guessed or reused.
Tricking users into clicking something on your site by showing it invisibly inside another site's page.
Splitting a long list into pages by passing a token that marks the last item seen, rather than a page number or offset.
A unique ID a client sends with a request so that, if it retries, the server recognises the repeat and doesn't do the work twice.
Letting anyone edit, but rejecting a save if the item changed since you read it (checked with a version label such as an ETag).
A small random extra wait added before a retry, so many clients don't all retry at the same instant.
A standard file format describing an HTTP API's endpoints, inputs and outputs, from which tools generate documentation and client code.
A value made with a private key that anyone with the matching public key can check, proving who made the data and that it wasn't changed.
A named combination of encryption methods that client and server agree to use for a TLS connection.
A single-use public key each side sends during the TLS handshake so both can compute the same secret key without sending it.
The hostname a client puts in its first TLS message, so a server hosting many sites knows which certificate to present.
A site's certificate plus the certificates that signed it, leading up to a root certificate the device already trusts.
A property of TLS: recorded traffic stays unreadable even if the server's private key is stolen later, because each session used throwaway keys.
Sending the first request together with the opening handshake on a resumed TLS/QUIC connection; fast, but the data can be replayed.
An attacker capturing a valid message and sending it again, for example to repeat a payment.
A lifetime a cache works out for itself when a response has no Cache-Control or Expires, often a fraction of its age since Last-Modified.
A Cache-Control option letting a cache keep serving an expired copy for a short time while it fetches a fresh one in the background.
Time to first byte: how long after sending a request the first byte of the response arrives.

concepts.name: Anatomy of a URL
concepts.summary: Take a web address apart: scheme, host, port, path, query and fragment, and why some characters must be encoded.
concepts.why: Every visit to a page and every call to an online service starts from an address, and many mistakes come from building one wrongly.
concepts.body:
When you type an address into a **browser** (the app you use to visit websites, like Chrome or Safari), it fetches a page from a **server**: a computer somewhere on the internet whose job is to wait for requests and answer them. The program asking, here your browser, is called the **client**.

That address is a **URL**. Take `https://shop.example.com:8443/products/shoes?color=red&page=2#reviews` and read it left to right:

- **scheme** `https`: which set of rules to talk by. Such an agreed set of rules is a **protocol**. The web's protocol is **HTTP**; **HTTPS** is HTTP with the conversation scrambled so nobody in between can read it.
- **host** `shop.example.com`: which server. This human-friendly name is a **domain name**; a later lesson shows how it's turned into the server's numeric address.
- **port** `8443`: which "door" on that server to knock on, since one machine can run several services. Usually left out: `https` means door 443, `http` means 80.
- **path** `/products/shoes`: which thing on that server you want, written like folders. Anything a URL points to (a page, an image, a list of products) is called a **resource**.
- **query** `?color=red&page=2`: extra options as `name=value` pairs joined by `&`, often for searching, filtering or choosing a page of results. This part is the **query string**.
- **fragment** `#reviews`: a spot within the page. The browser uses it itself and **never sends it to the server**.

Scheme, host and port together are the page's **origin**, `https://shop.example.com:8443`. Browsers use the origin to keep different websites apart, as later lessons show.

A URL may only contain plain English letters, digits and a few punctuation marks. Anything else must be written as `%` plus a code, which is called **URL encoding**: a space becomes `%20`, an `&` inside a value becomes `%26`, and `é` becomes `%C3%A9`. In query strings a space is often written `+` instead. That's why you shouldn't build URLs by gluing text together by hand: a value like `fish & chips` would break the query. Tools and programming languages have ready-made helpers that encode correctly.

A link can also leave parts out, like `/login` or `../img/a.png`. These are filled in from the URL of the page you're on.
concepts.code:
https://shop.example.com:8443/products/shoes?color=red&page=2#reviews
\___/   \______________/ \__/\_____________/ \________________/ \_____/
scheme      host         port      path            query        fragment

origin   = https://shop.example.com:8443
fragment = used by the browser only, never sent to the server

# Searching for "fish & chips" in Zürich, correctly encoded:
https://example.com/search?q=fish+%26+chips&city=Z%C3%BCrich
#   space -> +   & -> %26   ü -> %C3%BC

# A short link on the page https://site.com/blog/post/
../img/a.png   ->   https://site.com/blog/img/a.png
takeaways: A URL reads scheme://host:port/path?query#fragment
Origin = scheme + host + port
The fragment is never sent to the server
Special characters in values must be URL-encoded
pitfalls: Gluing typed-in text straight into a query string, so an `&` or `#` in the value breaks the URL.

quiz.q: Which part of https://shop.com/cart?id=5#summary is NOT sent to the server?
quiz.explain: The fragment is used by the browser itself and never leaves it.

quiz.q: What is the origin of https://app.example.com/settings?tab=2?
quiz.explain: The origin is scheme + host + port; the port here is the default 443, so it isn't written.

concepts.name: The request/response cycle
concepts.summary: See what an HTTP request and response actually look like: a first line, headers, a blank line and an optional body.
concepts.why: Once you can read the raw messages, every tool, error message and web problem becomes easier to understand.
concepts.body:
Every time a page loads, the client and server swap messages. The client sends a **request** ("please give me /products/shoes") and the server sends back exactly one **response** ("here it is", or "not found").

Each request stands on its own: the server doesn't remember earlier ones. A protocol that works like this is **stateless**. When a website does remember you, for example that you're logged in, it's because something is sent along with every request, usually a **cookie** (a small note the server asked the browser to keep and send back; see the cookies lesson).

The messages are plain text you can read. A request has:

- a **request line**: what to do, which resource, and the HTTP version, such as `GET /users/42 HTTP/1.1`. `GET` ("fetch this") is the **HTTP method**; the methods lesson covers the others.
- **headers**: extra details, one per line as `Name: value`. Each such line is a **header**. `Host: example.com` says which website is meant, because one server can host many.
- an empty line
- an optional **body**: the data being sent, such as the contents of a form you filled in

A response looks the same:

- a **status line**: the version, a three-digit **status code** saying how it went, and a short phrase, such as `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` or `404 Not Found`
- headers, such as `Content-Type: text/html` (what kind of data follows)
- an empty line, then the body: the page, a picture, some data

Newer versions, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, pack the same parts more compactly, but the meaning is identical, so everything here carries over.

You can watch real messages. In your browser, open the developer tools (F12, or right-click and choose Inspect) and pick the Network tab: it lists every request a page makes, with its headers and response. Or open a **terminal**, a window where you type commands, and use **curl**, a small program that sends a request and prints what comes back. `curl -v https://example.com/` shows the request lines marked `>` and the response lines marked `<`.
concepts.code:
$ curl -v https://example.com/        # shortened sample output
> GET / HTTP/2                        # the request: method, path, version
> Host: example.com                   # request headers...
> User-Agent: curl/8.11.0             # (which program is asking)
> Accept: */*                         # (any kind of reply is fine)
>                                     # blank line: end of the request
< HTTP/2 200                          # the response: status code 200 = OK
< content-type: text/html             # response headers...
< content-length: 1256                # (size of the body in bytes)
<                                     # blank line, then the body:
<!doctype html>
<html> ...

# The same request written out as plain HTTP/1.1 text:
#   GET / HTTP/1.1
#   Host: example.com
#   Accept: */*
#   (blank line)
takeaways: Request = method + path + headers + optional body
Response = status code + headers + optional body
HTTP is stateless: each request stands alone
`curl -v` and the browser's Network tab show the real messages
pitfalls: Assuming the server remembers your previous request; anything it should know must be sent again, for example in a cookie.

quiz.q: Why does every request include a Host header?
options: One server can host many websites, so it says which one is meant
It tells the server the client's address
quiz.explain: Many sites can share one server, so the server needs to be told which site the request is for.

quiz.q: A server answers with `HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found`. Which part is the status code?
quiz.explain: The three-digit number is the status code; "Not Found" is just a readable phrase next to it.

concepts.name: DNS: finding the server
concepts.summary: Follow how a name like example.com is turned into a server's numeric address, what DNS records hold, and why changes take time to spread.
concepts.why: This lookup is the first step of every visit, and the cause of many "site is down" and "my change isn't live yet" problems.
concepts.body:
Computers on the internet find each other by number, not by name. Each one has an **IP address**, like `93.184.215.14` (the older, shorter IPv4 style) or `2606:2800:21f:cb07::1` (the newer IPv6 style). Before your browser can contact `www.example.com`, it must find out that name's IP address.

That's the job of **DNS**, the Domain Name System: the internet's phone book. Looking a name up goes like this:

- Your computer first checks whether it already knows the answer from a recent lookup. A store of recent answers kept to save time is called a **cache**.
- If not, it asks a **resolver**: a DNS server run by your internet provider, or a public one such as 1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8.
- If the resolver doesn't know either, it asks around in steps: a root server points it to the servers for `.com`, which point it to the servers run for `example.com`, which give the final answer.

Every answer comes with a **TTL** (time to live): how many seconds it may be kept in a cache before asking again.

The answers are stored as DNS records, which come in different **record types**:

- `A` and `AAAA`: the IPv4 and IPv6 address for the name
- `CNAME`: "this name is really that other name", like a forwarding address
- `MX`: where email for the domain goes; `TXT`: free text, often used to prove you own a domain
- `HTTPS`: newer records with hints on how best to connect

TTLs explain why DNS changes seem slow. After you change a record, caches everywhere keep giving the old answer until their copy's TTL runs out. If you plan to move a site to a new server, lower the TTL a day before.

Ordinary DNS lookups are sent in the clear, so anyone on the network can see which sites you look up. Newer forms, DNS over HTTPS and DNS over TLS, hide them with **encryption**: scrambling data with a secret key so only the intended recipient can read it.

In a terminal, the command `dig` asks DNS directly and shows the answers, as in the example.
concepts.code:
# dig asks DNS for a name and prints the answer (sample output; real addresses vary)
$ dig +short www.github.com
github.com.            # a CNAME: www.github.com is really github.com
140.82.121.3           # the A record: github.com's IP address

$ dig shop.example.com A +noall +answer
shop.example.com.    300    IN    A    203.0.113.10
#                    ^ TTL: this answer may be cached for 300 seconds

$ dig gmail.com MX +short       # where gmail.com's email is delivered
5 gmail-smtp-in.l.google.com.

$ dig +trace www.wikipedia.org  # show each step: root -> .org -> wikipedia's servers
takeaways: DNS turns names into IP addresses, asking step by step when needed
A/AAAA = address, CNAME = other name, MX = email, TXT = text
The TTL says how long an answer may be cached, so how fast changes spread
Lower TTLs before a planned switch to a new server
pitfalls: Changing a DNS record that has a 24-hour TTL and expecting visitors to reach the new server immediately.

quiz.q: You change an A record whose TTL was 86400. Some users still reach the old server hours later. Why?
options: DNS changes need a server restart
Resolvers may keep the old answer cached for up to 24 hours
quiz.explain: A TTL of 86400 seconds lets caches keep the old record for a full day.

concepts.name: HTTP methods
concepts.summary: Use GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE for what they mean, and learn which requests are safe to repeat.
concepts.why: The method tells browsers, servers and every program in between what a request may change, and whether it's safe to send again.
concepts.body:
The first word of a request, the method, says what the client wants done with the resource:

- **GET**: send me this. It only reads.
- `HEAD`: like GET, but send only the headers, to check that something exists or how big it is.
- **POST**: here's some data, do something with it: create a new item, submit a form, start an action.
- `PUT`: replace the resource at this URL with what I send, creating it if it isn't there.
- `PATCH`: change just part of it.
- `DELETE`: remove it.
- `OPTIONS`: what am I allowed to do here? Browsers send it on their own for a safety check covered in the CORS lesson.

Two features matter more than the names.

A **safe method** promises not to change anything on the server: GET, HEAD and OPTIONS. Anything a request changes besides sending back an answer is called a **side effect**. Programs that roam the web (search engines' crawlers, link previews) send GET requests freely, so a GET link that deletes data will sooner or later be clicked by a robot.

A method is **idempotent** if sending it twice has the same effect as sending it once: the safe ones, plus PUT and DELETE. Deleting an item twice still leaves it deleted. That matters because networks fail. When a request gets no answer within a time limit (a **timeout**), the client can't tell whether it arrived. Idempotent requests can simply be sent again, which is called a **retry**.

POST and PATCH are not idempotent in general: retrying a POST might create two orders. That's why payment services ask for an extra unique ID with each payment (see the lesson on pagination, idempotency and versioning).

Idempotent doesn't mean the answer is the same: a second DELETE may answer "not found". And an ordinary HTML form on a web page can only send GET or POST; programs can send any method.
concepts.code:
GET /articles HTTP/1.1                 # read: the list of articles
Host: api.example.com

POST /articles HTTP/1.1                # create a new article from the body
Host: api.example.com
Content-Type: application/json

{"title": "Hello"}

PUT /articles/42 HTTP/1.1              # replace article 42 completely
Host: api.example.com
Content-Type: application/json

{"title": "Hello", "body": "...", "tags": []}

PATCH /articles/42 HTTP/1.1            # change only the title
Host: api.example.com
Content-Type: application/merge-patch+json

{"title": "Hello again"}

DELETE /articles/42 HTTP/1.1           # remove it; safe to send again
Host: api.example.com
takeaways: GET reads, POST creates or handles data, PUT replaces, PATCH changes part, DELETE removes
Safe methods change nothing: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS
Idempotent = repeating has the same effect: the safe methods plus PUT and DELETE
Never change data in response to a GET
pitfalls: Making a link like `GET /items/5/delete`, which robots and link previews will happily follow.

quiz.q: A request times out and the client doesn't know if it was processed. Which method is safe to send again automatically?
quiz.explain: PUT is idempotent: sending the same replacement twice leaves the same result.

concepts.name: Status codes
concepts.summary: Read the three-digit status code by its first digit: 2xx success, 3xx go elsewhere, 4xx the request was wrong, 5xx the server failed.
concepts.why: Browsers, search engines and monitoring tools act on the status code before they even look at the body.
concepts.body:
Every response starts with a status code that sums up how it went. The first digit gives the group:

**2xx: success.**

- `200 OK`; `201 Created` (a new item was made, and a `Location` header gives its URL); `202 Accepted` (taken on, will be done later); `204 No Content` (done, nothing to send back).

**3xx: look elsewhere.** These are **redirects**: the response names another URL in its `Location` header, and the browser goes there.

- `301 Moved Permanently` and `308 Permanent Redirect`: the resource has a new home for good.
- `302 Found` and `307 Temporary Redirect`: for now, go there instead.
- The difference within each pair: after 301 or 302, a browser may switch a POST into a GET; 307 and 308 guarantee the same method and body are sent again.
- `303 See Other`: go GET this other page, the usual answer after a form is submitted.
- `304 Not Modified`: the copy you already have is still good (see caching).

**4xx: the request needs fixing.**

- `400 Bad Request`, `404 Not Found`, `405 Method Not Allowed`, `409 Conflict`, `410 Gone`, `415 Unsupported Media Type`, `422 Unprocessable Content` (understood, but the data is invalid), `429 Too Many Requests`.
- `401 Unauthorized` really means "who are you?": not logged in, or the login details are wrong. Proving who you are is called **authentication**.
- `403 Forbidden` means "I know who you are, and you may not".

**5xx: the server failed.**

- `500 Internal Server Error`; `503 Service Unavailable` (overwhelmed or under maintenance, often with a `Retry-After` header).
- `502 Bad Gateway` and `504 Gateway Timeout`: a go-between server, which passes requests on to the real one, got a broken answer or none in time.

Choose precisely. Programs retry after 503 or 429 but not after 400, monitoring raises alarms on 5xx, and search engines remove pages that answer 404 or 410 from their results. Answering `200 OK` with an error message in the body breaks all of that.
concepts.code:
GET /old-page HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com

HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently        # 3xx: look elsewhere, for good
Location: /new-page                   # the browser now requests /new-page

GET /admin HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com

HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden                # 4xx: we know you, but you may not

GET /nope HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found                # 4xx: nothing at this URL
Content-Type: text/plain

not found

HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable      # 5xx: server trouble, try later
Retry-After: 120                      # ...in 120 seconds
takeaways: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx the request was wrong, 5xx the server failed
401 = not logged in (who are you?), 403 = logged in but not allowed
307/308 keep the method; 303 switches to GET
Never answer 200 for an error
pitfalls: Answering 200 with an error message in the body, which hides the failure from browsers, programs and monitoring.

quiz.q: A logged-in user asks for another user's private invoice. Which status fits best?
quiz.explain: The server knows who the user is, but they aren't allowed to see this. (Some sites answer 404 to hide that it exists.)

concepts.name: Headers
concepts.summary: Know the common request and response headers: how they describe the message, ask for a format, carry logins and control caching.
concepts.why: Almost every HTTP feature, from remembering logins to caching, is switched on by a header.
concepts.body:
Headers are the `Name: value` lines between the first line and the body. They are **metadata**, data about the message rather than the content itself, like the label on a parcel. Header names ignore upper and lower case (HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 send them all in lower case), and a program simply ignores headers it doesn't know. That's how new features get added without breaking old programs.

Common **request headers**:

- `Host`: which website. `User-Agent`: which program is asking (a browser name, `curl`).
- `Accept`, `Accept-Language`: which formats and languages the client prefers. The server picks the best match it has; this is called **content negotiation**.
- `Accept-Encoding: gzip, br, zstd`: which kinds of **compression** (shrinking data for the trip, like a zip file) the client can unpack.
- `Authorization`: proof of who you are, such as a password or a key. Such secret proof is called **credentials**.
- `Cookie`: the cookies stored for this site.
- `Content-Type` and `Content-Length`: what kind of body is attached, and its size.
- `If-None-Match`, `If-Modified-Since`: "only send it if it changed" (see caching).
- `Referer` (misspelt in the standard): the page whose link led here. `Origin`: the origin of the page making the request.

Common **response headers**:

- `Content-Type`, `Content-Length`, and `Content-Encoding` (which compression was used, such as `br`).
- `Cache-Control`, `ETag`, `Last-Modified`, `Vary`: whether and how long the response may be kept in a cache.
- `Location` for redirects and newly created items; `Set-Cookie` to store a cookie.
- `Retry-After` with 429 or 503.

Anyone can invent headers. They used to start with `X-` (`X-Request-Id`); new ones shouldn't, but many old `X-` names live on.

Headers have size limits: servers usually accept about 8 to 16 **kilobytes** (thousands of bytes, a byte being one character of plain text) in total. Huge cookies can cause `431 Request Header Fields Too Large`. See headers with `curl -I` (headers only) or `curl -v`, or in the browser's Network tab.
concepts.code:
# Ask for German, accept two kinds of compression, and show only the headers
$ curl -sI https://shop.example.com/ -H "Accept-Language: de" -H "Accept-Encoding: br, gzip"
# sample response (shortened)
HTTP/2 200
content-type: text/html; charset=utf-8
content-encoding: br                      # compressed with Brotli (br)
content-language: de                      # the German version was chosen
cache-control: no-cache
vary: Accept-Encoding, Accept-Language    # the answer depended on these headers
etag: "5f2c-9a1"

# -H adds a request header of your own
$ curl -sI https://example.com -H "X-Request-Id: abc123"
takeaways: Header names ignore case; HTTP/2 and later send them in lower case
Accept-* headers let the server choose the best format or language
Logins, cookies, caching and redirects are all controlled by headers
Oversized headers cause 431 errors
pitfalls: Assuming a header name's capital letters matter when you look for it.

quiz.q: A client sends Accept-Encoding: br, gzip. What may the server do?
options: Compress the body with Brotli or gzip and say which in Content-Encoding
quiz.explain: Accept-Encoding lists the compression the client can unpack; Content-Encoding says which one was used.

concepts.name: Bodies and content types
concepts.summary: Label a message's body with Content-Type so the other side can read it: JSON, form data, file uploads, text and images.
concepts.why: A missing or wrong content type is behind countless "400 Bad Request" and "the data arrived empty" problems.
concepts.body:
A body is just a sequence of **bytes** (small numbers from 0 to 255). On their own, bytes could be text, a picture or anything else. The `Content-Type` header tells the recipient how to read them, using a **MIME type** (also called a media type) such as `text/html` or `image/png`, sometimes with extra details after a `;`.

The ones you'll see most:

- `text/html; charset=utf-8`: a web page, written in **HTML** (the language web pages are made of). `charset` names the **encoding**, the rule for turning letters into bytes; **UTF-8** is the standard one that covers every language. Also `text/plain` and `text/css`.
- `application/json`: data in **JSON**, a simple text format like `{"name": "Ada", "langs": ["en", "fr"]}`. It's the usual format for a **web API**: a service built for programs, rather than people, to call over HTTP.
- `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`: what a plain HTML form sends, like `name=Ada&lang=en`.
- `multipart/form-data; boundary=...`: a form that includes file uploads. Each input of the form becomes a separate part, divided by a marker text, the boundary.
- `image/png`, `image/avif`, `video/mp4`, and `application/octet-stream` for "some bytes, type unknown". Content that isn't text, like these, is called **binary data**.

Servers decide how to read a request body from its `Content-Type`. If you send JSON without the header, many servers see nothing, or plain text; with an unsupported type and you get `415 Unsupported Media Type`.

The recipient learns the size from `Content-Length`. When the size isn't known in advance, the body is sent piece by piece as it's produced: in HTTP/1.1 this is called **chunked transfer encoding**; HTTP/2 and 3 have their own way.

`Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="report.pdf"` asks the browser to download the file rather than show it.

If a response has no type, or a vague one, browsers may guess from the content. That guessing can be abused, for example to make an uploaded "image" run as a program, so send `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and always give an accurate type, with `charset=utf-8` for text.
concepts.code:
POST /signup HTTP/1.1                  # JSON body: say so in Content-Type
Host: api.example.com
Content-Type: application/json

{"name": "Ada", "langs": ["en", "fr"]}

POST /signup HTTP/1.1                  # what a plain HTML form sends
Host: example.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

name=Ada+Lovelace&lang=en              # space written as +

POST /avatar HTTP/1.1                  # a form with a file upload
Host: example.com
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=XyZ

--XyZ
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="title"

Avatar
--XyZ
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="file"; filename="a.png"
Content-Type: image/png

(the image's bytes)
--XyZ--
takeaways: Content-Type tells the recipient how to read the body
APIs use application/json; forms use urlencoded or multipart
File uploads need multipart/form-data
Always send an accurate type, plus nosniff, on responses
pitfalls: Posting JSON without `Content-Type: application/json`, so the server doesn't read it as JSON.

quiz.q: A program sends JSON in a POST body but forgets the Content-Type header. What commonly happens?
options: The server always detects JSON by itself
The server doesn't read it as JSON, so the data seems missing or wrong
quiz.explain: Servers choose how to read a body from its Content-Type; without the right one, the JSON isn't understood as JSON.

quiz.q: Which content type should a form with a file upload use?
quiz.explain: multipart/form-data sends each field, including the file's bytes, as a separate part.

concepts.name: TCP, TLS and HTTPS
concepts.summary: Understand the connection under HTTP: the TCP handshake, the TLS handshake, certificates, and why HTTPS is the default.
concepts.why: Setting up a connection costs several trips across the network, and expired certificates are among the most common causes of outages.
concepts.body:
Before any HTTP message is sent, client and server need a connection. Data crosses the internet in small pieces called **packets**, which can get lost or arrive out of order. HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 run on **TCP**, a protocol that turns those packets into a reliable, ordered flow of bytes: it numbers them, puts them back in order and resends lost ones.

Opening a TCP connection takes a **handshake**, an opening exchange of three short messages (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK). That costs one **round trip**: a message there and a reply back, often written RTT (round-trip time). The delay of one round trip is the connection's **latency**. TCP also starts sending slowly and speeds up as things go well, so a new connection is slower than one that's been running.

**HTTPS** is HTTP sent inside **TLS**, a protocol that adds:

- encryption: nobody on the Wi-Fi or at an internet provider can read or change the traffic
- integrity: any tampering is detected
- proof of identity: the server proves it really is that domain, using a **certificate**

A certificate is the server's digital ID card. It's signed by a **certificate authority**, an organisation your browser trusts, whose list comes built in. The client checks that the certificate is for this exact hostname, hasn't expired, and was signed by a trusted authority.

The TLS 1.3 handshake adds one more round trip. In it the server sends its certificate, and both sides use a clever bit of maths to agree on a fresh secret key without ever sending the key itself. Let's Encrypt issues free certificates automatically, and certificates now last only months or weeks, so renew them automatically.

So a brand-new HTTPS request pays for the DNS lookup, then TCP (1 round trip), then TLS (1 round trip) before the request even leaves. At 100 ms per round trip that's 200 ms of pure setup. That's why reusing an open connection for many requests (keep-alive) matters, and why HTTP/3 merges the two handshakes.

Browsers mark plain HTTP pages "Not secure", and many browser features only work over HTTPS. Serve everything over HTTPS and redirect HTTP to it.
concepts.code:
# Time each step of a request (each time includes the steps before it)
$ curl -so /dev/null https://example.com -w \
  "dns %{time_namelookup}s\ntcp %{time_connect}s\ntls %{time_appconnect}s\nfirst byte %{time_starttransfer}s\n"
dns 0.012s
tcp 0.045s        # TCP handshake done
tls 0.091s        # TLS handshake done
first byte 0.140s # first byte of the response arrived

# openssl is a toolkit for TLS; this shows who the certificate is for,
# who signed it, and when it expires
$ openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
    | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -enddate
takeaways: HTTPS = HTTP inside TLS, on top of TCP
TCP handshake = 1 round trip; TLS 1.3 handshake = 1 more
Certificates prove domain ownership, signed by a trusted authority
Reuse connections and renew certificates automatically
pitfalls: Letting a certificate expire because renewing it was a manual job.

quiz.q: Ignoring DNS, how many round trips does a fresh HTTPS (TLS 1.3 over TCP) request need before the server sees the HTTP request?
quiz.explain: One round trip for the TCP handshake and one for the TLS 1.3 handshake; the request goes out right after.

concepts.name: Cookies and sessions
concepts.summary: Remember users across requests with Set-Cookie, and protect cookies with HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite, Domain, Path and expiry.
concepts.why: Logins work through cookies, and most stolen-login attacks exploit badly set cookie options.
concepts.body:
HTTP doesn't remember anything between requests, so a server gives the browser a cookie to send back. The response says `Set-Cookie: session=abc123; ...`, and from then on the browser adds `Cookie: session=abc123` to every request to that site.

A **session** is the server's memory of one visitor, such as "this is Ada, logged in". Usually the cookie holds only a long random ID that points to that memory on the server. Sometimes the cookie holds the data itself as a **token**: a string that proves something, signed so it can't be faked.

Pages can contain code in **JavaScript**, the programming language that runs inside web pages. That matters for cookies because of two classic attacks:

- **XSS** (cross-site scripting): an attacker gets their own JavaScript to run on your page, for example through a comment box that doesn't clean its input, and steals what the page can read.
- **CSRF** (cross-site request forgery): another site makes your browser send a request to a site you're logged into, and your cookie goes along with it.

The cookie's options decide how safe it is:

- `HttpOnly`: page JavaScript can't read it, so an XSS bug can't steal the session. Always set it on login cookies.
- `Secure`: only ever sent over HTTPS.
- `SameSite`: whether it's sent when the request comes from another site. `Lax` sends it when you follow a link to the site, but not with forms posted or content loaded from other sites, which blocks most CSRF. `Strict` never sends it from other sites. `None` always does, and requires `Secure`. Chrome treats a missing value as `Lax`, but set it explicitly.
- `Max-Age` or `Expires`: how long to keep it. Without them it's a **session cookie**, deleted when the browser closes.
- `Domain`: leave it out to keep the cookie on this exact host; `Domain=example.com` also shares it with every subdomain, like `shop.example.com`.
- `Path`: limits it to some URL paths; this is not a security boundary.

A name starting with `__Host-` forces `Secure`, no `Domain` and `Path=/`: the strictest setting.

Cookies travel with every matching request, so keep them small (browsers allow about 4 KB each). Most browsers block or restrict **third-party cookies** (set by other sites embedded in a page, like ad networks); don't rely on them.
concepts.code:
GET /login HTTP/1.1                    # 1. the user logs in
Host: example.com

HTTP/1.1 200 OK                        # 2. the server stores a cookie
Set-Cookie: __Host-session=r4nd0m1d; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Max-Age=3600

GET /me HTTP/1.1                       # 3. every later request carries it back
Host: example.com
Cookie: __Host-session=r4nd0m1d

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain

Hello, Ada
takeaways: Set-Cookie stores a cookie; Cookie sends it back
Login cookies: HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax at minimum
SameSite blocks most CSRF; SameSite=None requires Secure
Leave out Domain to keep a cookie on one host
pitfalls: Keeping login tokens in the browser's localStorage, a storage area any script on the page can read, instead of an HttpOnly cookie.

quiz.q: Which attribute stops JavaScript running on the page from reading a cookie?
quiz.explain: HttpOnly cookies are hidden from page JavaScript but still sent with requests.

concepts.name: HTTP caching basics
concepts.summary: Control how browsers and other caches keep responses with Cache-Control, and check cheaply for changes with ETag, Last-Modified and 304.
concepts.why: The fastest request is the one never made; the right caching headers cut load times and server costs dramatically.
concepts.body:
A cache keeps copies of responses to reuse them. Your browser has one, and there are **shared caches** used by many people, run by servers between you and the website, such as a **CDN** (a network of servers around the world that keep copies close to users; see the CDN lesson). The website controls all of them with response headers.

**Freshness.** `Cache-Control: max-age=3600` means "this may be reused for 3600 seconds (an hour) without asking me". While the copy is fresh, the browser doesn't send a request at all.

**Checking for changes.** Once the copy is too old (stale), the cache can ask "has it changed?" with a **conditional request**. If the response came with an **ETag**, a version label like `"v42"`, the cache sends `If-None-Match: "v42"`; if it came with `Last-Modified`, it sends `If-Modified-Since`. If nothing changed, the server answers `304 Not Modified` with no body, and the cached copy is used. This check is called **revalidation**: it saves sending the content again, though not the round trip.

The main `Cache-Control` options:

- `max-age=N` (all caches) and `s-maxage=N` (shared caches only)
- `no-cache`: you may keep it, but check with me before **every** use. Despite the name, it does cache.
- `no-store`: never keep it at all. For private data.
- `private`: only the user's own browser may keep it, not a shared cache. `public`: shared caches may keep it even where they normally wouldn't, such as for logged-in requests.
- `immutable`: this will never change while fresh, so don't even check on reload.

A standard plan:

- HTML pages: `no-cache`, so users always get the latest version, cheaply checked.
- Files such as scripts, styles and images, given a name that includes a **hash** of their contents (a short fingerprint computed from the bytes), like `app.3f9a1c.js`: `max-age=31536000, immutable`. A new version gets a new name, so an old copy never needs replacing.
concepts.code:
GET /price HTTP/1.1                    # first visit
Host: shop.example.com

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Cache-Control: no-cache                # keep it, but check before each use
ETag: "a1b2c3d4"                       # version label of this content
Content-Type: application/json

{"price": 12}

GET /price HTTP/1.1                    # later: "has it changed?"
Host: shop.example.com
If-None-Match: "a1b2c3d4"

HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified              # no: reuse your copy (no body sent)
ETag: "a1b2c3d4"
takeaways: max-age = reuse without asking; ETag/Last-Modified = cheap check answered with 304
no-cache means check every time; no-store means don't keep it
private keeps responses out of shared caches
Hashed file names + immutable for files, no-cache for HTML
pitfalls: Using no-cache when you meant no-store for private responses.

quiz.q: Which header makes a browser revalidate a response on every use, but still keep a copy?
quiz.explain: no-cache allows keeping a copy but requires checking with the server before each reuse.

concepts.name: Same-origin policy and CORS
concepts.summary: Understand why browsers stop pages from reading other sites' responses, and how servers allow it with Access-Control-Allow-* headers and preflight requests.
concepts.why: "Blocked by CORS policy" is the most common error people hit when a web page calls an API on another site.
concepts.body:
Page JavaScript can send requests to other sites. The **same-origin policy** is the browser rule that stops it from **reading** responses that come from a different origin (scheme + host + port). Without it, any website you visit could use your logged-in cookies to read your email from another tab.

**CORS** (cross-origin resource sharing) lets a server relax that rule for origins it chooses. The browser adds an `Origin` header to requests sent to another origin; the server answers with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com` (or `*` for anyone). If the answer doesn't match, the browser hides the response from the page's JavaScript. The request may still have reached the server: CORS protects reading, not sending.

**Preflight.** "Simple" requests (GET, HEAD, or a POST that looks like a plain form, with no special headers) are sent directly. Anything else, such as `PUT`, `DELETE`, a JSON `Content-Type` or an `Authorization` header, makes the browser first send an automatic `OPTIONS` request asking permission. This is the **preflight request**. The server must answer it with:

- `Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE`
- `Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type, Authorization`
- optionally `Access-Control-Max-Age: 600`, so the browser can remember the answer for 600 seconds

**Cookies across origins.** For cookies or other credentials to go along, the page's code must ask for it, and the server must answer `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` with the exact origin; `*` isn't allowed then. If the allowed origin differs per request, add `Vary: Origin` so caches don't mix up the answers.

Only browsers enforce CORS. curl, servers and phone apps ignore it, so it doesn't protect your data from anyone; it's not a permission system. A CORS error is always fixed on the server (or by a server on the page's own origin that passes requests on), never in the page's own code.
concepts.code:
# Browser at https://app.example.com wants to PUT JSON to the API
OPTIONS /items/7 HTTP/1.1               # 1. preflight, sent automatically
Host: api.example.com
Origin: https://app.example.com
Access-Control-Request-Method: PUT
Access-Control-Request-Headers: content-type

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content                 # 2. the server allows it
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: Content-Type, Authorization
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
Access-Control-Max-Age: 600
Vary: Origin

PUT /items/7 HTTP/1.1                   # 3. now the real request goes out
Host: api.example.com
Origin: https://app.example.com
Content-Type: application/json

{"name": "lamp"}
takeaways: The same-origin policy stops pages reading other origins' responses
Servers allow chosen origins with Access-Control-Allow-Origin
Non-simple requests trigger an OPTIONS preflight first
With cookies, name the exact origin (not *) and send Allow-Credentials
pitfalls: Trying to fix a CORS error in the page's code; the server must send the headers.
Treating CORS as protection for an API; programs other than browsers ignore it.

quiz.q: A page sends a POST with Content-Type: application/json to another origin. Before the POST goes out, what does the browser send?
options: Nothing; JSON is never allowed cross-origin
quiz.explain: application/json isn't a "simple" content type, so the browser asks permission first with an OPTIONS preflight.

concepts.name: Authentication over HTTP
concepts.summary: Send credentials with the Authorization header (Basic, Bearer tokens, API keys), and use 401, 403 and WWW-Authenticate correctly.
concepts.why: Every API you call or build needs to know who's calling, and HTTP's conventions decide how programs and tools handle it.
concepts.body:
HTTP has a standard way to prove who you are. The client sends `Authorization: <scheme> <credentials>`, where the scheme names the method. A server that wants credentials answers `401 Unauthorized` with a `WWW-Authenticate` header naming the scheme it accepts.

Common schemes:

- **Basic**: `Authorization: Basic` followed by `user:password` written in **base64**, a way of writing any bytes using only letters, digits and a few symbols. Base64 is not encryption: anyone can turn it back. So Basic is acceptable only over HTTPS. It's still used for simple internal tools.
- **Bearer**: `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. Whoever holds ("bears") the token is let in, so such an **access token** must be kept secret. It's often a **JWT** (JSON Web Token): a small piece of JSON saying who you are and when it expires, signed by the server so it can't be altered. Or it's a random string the server looks up. Tokens from OAuth, the system behind "Sign in with Google", use this scheme.
- **API keys**: a long secret string that identifies a program, often sent in a custom header such as `X-API-Key`. Don't put keys in the URL's query string: URLs end up in **logs** (the files where servers record each request), browser history and `Referer` headers.

In browsers, the main alternative is a login cookie. It travels automatically, which is convenient but needs CSRF protection (`SameSite`). A token that page JavaScript sends itself isn't exposed to CSRF, but it must be stored where scripts can read it, which exposes it to XSS.

Status codes: `401` means "who are you?" (credentials missing, wrong or expired: log in again or get a new token). `403` means "I know who you are, and no". A client making too many requests gets `429 Too Many Requests`; this cap is called a **rate limit**.

Always use HTTPS, make tokens expire soon, and never write Authorization headers into logs.
concepts.code:
# Basic: curl writes user:password in base64 for you
$ curl -u ada:s3cret https://api.example.com/me
# sends the header:  Authorization: Basic YWRhOnMzY3JldA==
$ echo -n 'ada:s3cret' | base64        # anyone can do the same, or undo it
YWRhOnMzY3JldA==

# Bearer token (-H adds a header)
$ curl -H "Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdWIiOiI0MiJ9.sig" \
       https://api.example.com/me

# A server asking for credentials (-i shows the response headers)
$ curl -si https://api.example.com/me | head -3
HTTP/2 401
www-authenticate: Bearer realm="api", error="invalid_token"
content-type: application/json
takeaways: Authorization: <scheme> <credentials>; 401 + WWW-Authenticate asks for them
Basic is base64, not encryption: HTTPS only
Bearer tokens let in whoever holds them
401 = not identified, 403 = not allowed
pitfalls: Putting API keys in the URL's query string, where they leak into logs and Referer headers.

quiz.q: What does the Basic credential 'YWRhOnMzY3JldA==' protect against on plain HTTP?
quiz.explain: Base64 can be turned back by anyone, so Basic auth relies entirely on HTTPS.

concepts.name: Designing REST APIs
concepts.summary: Design an API around resources and URLs, map actions to methods and status codes, and return consistent JSON and errors.
concepts.why: A predictable API is easier to use, document, cache and change than a pile of one-off URLs.
concepts.body:
**REST**, in everyday use, means designing a web API around resources named by URLs, acted on with the standard methods, and sent as JSON. Each URL-and-method combination the API offers, like `GET /articles`, is an **endpoint**.

**URLs name things; methods say what to do:**

- `GET /articles` lists them; `POST /articles` creates one and answers `201` with a `Location` header.
- `GET /articles/42` reads one; `PATCH` or `PUT /articles/42` updates it; `DELETE /articles/42` deletes it (`204`).
- Resources that belong to another show it in the path: `GET /articles/42/comments`.
- Use plural nouns, lower case and hyphens: `/order-items`, not `/getOrderItems`.

Actions that don't fit can become resources (`POST /orders/7/cancellation`) or, pragmatically, `POST /orders/7/cancel`.

**Query strings** handle filtering, sorting and splitting long lists into pages, called **pagination**: `GET /articles?author=ada&sort=-published_at&limit=20` (the `-` means newest first).

**Consistent errors**: use the right status code and the same body shape every time. A standard shape exists, Problem Details, defined in RFC 9457 (RFCs are the numbered documents that define internet standards). It's sent as `application/problem+json`, with `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail` and room for extra fields, such as which input was wrong.

**Other conventions**:

- Pick one style for JSON field names, `first_name` or `firstName`, and stick to it.
- Write dates and times in the **ISO 8601** format in **UTC**, the world's standard time zone: `2026-10-17T09:30:00Z`.
- Send back the created or updated item, so clients don't need another request.
- Describe the API in an **OpenAPI** file, from which tools generate documentation, tests and ready-made client code.

Design from the caller's point of view: what will their screens and programs actually need, and in how many requests?
concepts.code:
POST /v1/articles HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{"title": "HTTP caching", "tags": ["web"]}

HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /v1/articles/42
Content-Type: application/json

{"id": 42, "title": "HTTP caching", "tags": ["web"], "created_at": "2026-10-17T09:30:00Z"}

GET /v1/articles?tag=web&sort=-created_at&limit=20 HTTP/1.1

PATCH /v1/articles/42 HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{"title": ""}

HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Content
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{"type": "https://api.example.com/errors/validation", "title": "Invalid article",
 "status": 422, "errors": [{"field": "title", "detail": "must not be empty"}]}
takeaways: Nouns in URLs, actions as methods
201 + Location for creation, 204 for success with nothing to return
Filtering, sorting and paging go in the query string
Use one error format, such as application/problem+json
pitfalls: Action-style URLs like `POST /getUser` or `GET /deleteUser?id=5`.

quiz.q: Which is the most RESTful way to list the comments of article 42?
quiz.explain: Comments belong to the article, so they're read with GET at a path under it.

concepts.name: HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
concepts.summary: How HTTP/2 sends many requests over one connection at once, why HTTP/3 moved to QUIC over UDP, and what that changes for you.
concepts.why: The protocol version decides which speed tricks help or hurt, from splitting files across domains to bundling them together.
concepts.body:
**HTTP/1.1** sends one request at a time on a connection, and a slow response holds up everything queued behind it. This is called **head-of-line blocking**, like one slow shopper at a single checkout. Browsers work around it by opening about six connections per origin. Developers used to add more tricks: bundling many files into one, combining small images into one big image, and spreading files across several domain names to get more connections.

**HTTP/2** (2015) keeps the same methods, headers and status codes, but changes how they travel:

- Messages are cut into binary pieces (frames), and each request-response pair becomes a separate numbered **stream**. Many streams share one TCP connection, their frames interleaved. Carrying many conversations over one connection like this is **multiplexing**, so one slow response no longer holds up the others at the HTTP level.
- **HPACK** compresses headers, which matters because cookies and other headers repeat on every request.
- Clients can hint which responses matter most, now mostly through the `Priority` header.
- Browsers use it only over TLS. Which version to speak is agreed during the TLS handshake through **ALPN**, where the client lists the protocols it knows (`h2` means HTTP/2).

But TCP still delivers bytes strictly in order. One lost packet holds up *all* streams until it's resent, which hurts on patchy mobile networks.

**HTTP/3** (2022) runs on **QUIC**, a newer transport built on **UDP**, a simple protocol that just sends packets without TCP's ordering:

- Streams are independent all the way down, so a lost packet only holds up its own stream.
- TLS 1.3 is built in, so connecting and encrypting happen in a single round trip; a returning client can even send its first request immediately (0-RTT).
- A connection survives switching from Wi-Fi to mobile data, because it's identified by an ID rather than by the IP addresses and ports.

Servers announce HTTP/3 support with the `Alt-Svc` response header or a DNS `HTTPS` record, and browsers then switch. For you: serve over HTTP/2 or 3, stop spreading files across extra domains, and bundle files only as much as makes sense for caching.
concepts.code:
# Which version does a site use? (-w prints details after the request)
$ curl -sI --http2 https://www.cloudflare.com -o /dev/null -w "%{http_version}\n"
2

# Does it announce HTTP/3?
$ curl -sI https://www.cloudflare.com | grep -i alt-svc
alt-svc: h3=":443"; ma=86400            # h3 = HTTP/3, on port 443, for 86400 s

# Try HTTP/3 directly (needs a curl built with HTTP/3 support)
$ curl -sI --http3-only https://www.cloudflare.com -o /dev/null -w "%{http_version}\n"
3

# In the browser's Network tab: right-click the column headings and enable "Protocol" (h2, h3)
takeaways: HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection
A lost TCP packet still holds up every HTTP/2 stream
HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP: independent streams, built-in TLS 1.3, connections that survive network changes
Alt-Svc or a DNS HTTPS record announces HTTP/3
pitfalls: Keeping the old trick of spreading files over many domains, which defeats HTTP/2's single connection and adds handshakes.

quiz.q: What problem does HTTP/3 solve that HTTP/2 cannot?
options: A lost packet holding up every stream
quiz.explain: HTTP/2's streams share one strictly ordered TCP connection; QUIC's streams are independent.

concepts.name: WebSockets and server-sent events
concepts.summary: Let the server send data the moment it has it, with server-sent events (one way) or WebSockets (both ways).
concepts.why: Chats, notifications, live dashboards and shared editing all need the server to speak first.
concepts.body:
In plain HTTP only the client starts a conversation; the server can only answer. For live updates there are three main options.

**Polling**: ask "anything new?" every few seconds. Simple, but wasteful and always a little late. **Long polling** improves on it: the server holds the request open until there's news, then answers.

**Server-sent events (SSE)**: the client makes one ordinary GET. The server answers `Content-Type: text/event-stream` and keeps the response open, writing each event as a few lines of text:

```text
event: price
data: {"symbol":"ACME","value":12.5}
```

followed by a blank line. In the browser, JavaScript's `EventSource` reads them, **reconnects automatically**, and on reconnecting sends the last event's `id` in a `Last-Event-ID` header so nothing is missed. SSE is one-way (server to client), text only, and works with ordinary HTTP servers. Over HTTP/1.1 each open stream uses up one of the browser's ~6 connections per origin; HTTP/2 removes that limit. AI chat services stream their answers word by word this way.

**WebSockets**: a lasting two-way channel. The client sends a GET with `Upgrade: websocket` and a `Sec-WebSocket-Key` header; the server answers `101 Switching Protocols`. From then on the connection no longer speaks HTTP: either side can send messages at any time, as text or as binary data, with very little extra data per message. Use `wss://`, the TLS-protected form. You must handle reconnecting, regular "still there?" messages (heartbeats) and your message format yourself. Any go-between servers, such as the load balancers that spread traffic over several servers, must allow the upgrade and long-lived connections.

Rule of thumb: SSE for feeds from server to client; WebSockets when the client also sends often (chat, games, shared editing). The newer WebTransport, over HTTP/3, aims at similar uses with several streams per connection.
concepts.code:
# Server-sent events: one GET, one long response
GET /events HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Accept: text/event-stream

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/event-stream
Cache-Control: no-cache

id: 1
event: tick
data: {"n": 1}
                                        # blank line ends each event
id: 2
event: tick
data: {"n": 2}

# WebSocket: ask to switch protocols
GET /chat HTTP/1.1
Host: chat.example.com
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==
Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13

HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols        # from here on: WebSocket messages, both ways
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Accept: s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=
takeaways: SSE = one long GET with text/event-stream; reconnects itself; server to client only
WebSockets switch over with 101 Switching Protocols to a two-way channel
Use SSE for feeds, WebSockets for busy two-way traffic
Go-between servers must allow long-lived connections
pitfalls: Using WebSockets for a one-way notification feed, then rebuilding the reconnection that SSE gives for free.

quiz.q: Which status code does a server send to accept a WebSocket handshake?
quiz.explain: The connection is switched from HTTP to the WebSocket protocol with 101.

concepts.name: CDNs, proxies and load balancers
concepts.summary: See how reverse proxies, load balancers and CDNs sit between users and your servers, and how caching headers control what a CDN keeps.
concepts.why: Almost every real website is served through these layers, and how they behave depends on your HTTP headers.
concepts.body:
Requests rarely go straight to the program that builds your pages.

A **reverse proxy** (nginx, HAProxy, Envoy, Caddy) is a server that receives the visitors' connections and passes each request on to your application servers behind it, called the **backend**. It handles TLS (so the backend doesn't have to), compresses responses, serves fixed files such as images directly, enforces limits and adds headers. A load balancer is a reverse proxy that spreads requests over several backend servers, regularly checking which ones are healthy.

Behind a proxy, your application sees the proxy's IP address, not the visitor's. The original details travel in the `Forwarded` header, or the widely used `X-Forwarded-For`, `X-Forwarded-Proto` and `X-Forwarded-Host`. Trust them only when your own proxy set them; anyone can send fake ones.

A CDN (Cloudflare, Fastly, CloudFront, Akamai) runs reverse proxies in hundreds of places worldwide, called **edge servers**. Visitors connect to a nearby edge, which makes the TCP and TLS handshakes faster, and the edge either answers from its cache or fetches from your own server, the **origin server**.

The CDN's cache follows your headers:

- `Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=600` lets shared caches keep a response for 10 minutes, while browsers follow `max-age`.
- `private` or `no-store` keeps responses with personal data off the edge. Requests with cookies or an `Authorization` header usually skip the CDN cache by default.
- `Vary` makes the cache keep separate copies per value of a request header, such as `Vary: Accept-Encoding`.
- The `Age` header shows how long a copy has been cached; CDNs add their own hit-or-miss header, such as `cf-cache-status`.

Removing copies from a CDN early ("purging") is possible but slow and easy to get wrong; file names containing a content hash avoid the need. CDNs also soak up floods of junk traffic meant to knock a site offline, and can run small programs at the edge.
concepts.code:
# Is the response served from the CDN's cache?
$ curl -sI https://www.example-shop.com/assets/app.3f9a1c.js | grep -iE "cache-control|age|cache-status"
cache-control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
age: 48211                     # this copy has been cached for 48211 seconds
cf-cache-status: HIT           # served from the edge, not the origin

# Part of an nginx reverse-proxy setup for an app running on port 3000
#   location / {
#     proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000;                          # pass requests on
#     proxy_set_header Host $host;                               # keep the original host
#     proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;  # visitor's IP
#     proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;                # http or https
#   }
takeaways: Reverse proxies handle TLS and pass requests to the backend
Trust X-Forwarded-* only from your own proxy
CDN edges cache according to your Cache-Control (s-maxage for shared caches)
Keep personal responses private or no-store
pitfalls: Letting the CDN cache a personal page publicly, so one user's data is shown to others.

quiz.q: Which directive lets a CDN cache a page for 10 minutes while browsers revalidate every time?
quiz.explain: s-maxage applies only to shared caches, and no-cache makes browsers check every time.

concepts.name: HTTPS everywhere and security headers
concepts.summary: Harden a site with HSTS, Content-Security-Policy, frame protection, Referrer-Policy and safe cookie settings.
concepts.why: A handful of response headers block whole families of attacks, such as being pushed back to plain HTTP, XSS and clickjacking.
concepts.body:
Beyond TLS itself, several response headers tell browsers to enforce stricter rules.

**HSTS** (`Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload`) tells the browser to use only HTTPS for this domain for the next two years, even if someone types `http://`. That stops an attacker on public Wi-Fi from quietly keeping a visitor on plain HTTP. Make sure every subdomain supports HTTPS first; it's hard to undo.

**CSP** (`Content-Security-Policy`) lists where scripts, styles, images and connections may come from, so an XSS bug can't easily run the attacker's code. A strict policy uses a **nonce**, a random value made fresh for every response: `script-src 'nonce-r4nd0m' 'strict-dynamic'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'`, with the same value on each `<script>` tag you wrote yourself. An injected script won't have it. Start with `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only`, which reports violations without blocking anything.

**Clickjacking** means placing your page invisibly inside another site's page (in a frame, an `<iframe>`) and tricking visitors into clicking your buttons. `frame-ancestors 'none'` in CSP (or the older `X-Frame-Options: DENY`) forbids other sites from framing yours.

**Others**:

- `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`: never guess a response's type.
- `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin` (browsers' default): don't reveal full URLs to other sites.
- `Permissions-Policy: camera=(), geolocation=()`: switch off browser features you don't use.
- `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin`: cut the link between your window and pop-ups from other origins.

Combine these with cookies set `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite`. Check a site's headers in the browser's developer tools, or with scanners such as Mozilla's HTTP Observatory.
concepts.code:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains
Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'nonce-q8Zt3c1Lr2' 'strict-dynamic'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin
Permissions-Policy: camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=()
Set-Cookie: __Host-session=r4nd0m1d; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

<!doctype html><title>Safe</title>
<script nonce="q8Zt3c1Lr2">console.log("allowed: has this response's nonce")</script>
<script>console.log("blocked by CSP: no nonce")</script>
takeaways: HSTS forces HTTPS on future visits
CSP with a nonce limits which scripts can run, containing XSS
frame-ancestors 'none' prevents clickjacking
Roll out CSP in Report-Only mode first
pitfalls: Enabling HSTS with includeSubDomains before every subdomain supports HTTPS.

quiz.q: What does Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none' prevent?
options: Other sites embedding your page in a frame
quiz.explain: frame-ancestors controls who may show your page in a frame, which defeats clickjacking.

concepts.name: Pagination, idempotency and versioning
concepts.summary: Handle long lists, safe retries, request limits and API changes with cursor pagination, idempotency keys, 429 and versioning.
concepts.why: These patterns are what let an API survive real clients, retries and change instead of breaking under them.
concepts.body:
**Pagination.** Never return endless lists.

- Offset pagination (`?limit=20&offset=40`, "skip 40, give me 20") is simple and lets you jump to page N. But it gets slow on huge tables, and items shift between pages when data changes.
- **Cursor pagination** (`?limit=20&after=eyJpZCI6NDJ9`) passes a token marking the last item seen. It stays correct and fast, which suits feeds and endless scrolling.
- Return the next cursor in the body, or in a `Link: <...>; rel="next"` header.

**Idempotency keys.** POST isn't idempotent, but networks fail halfway through. So the client makes up a unique ID for each logical operation and sends it in an `Idempotency-Key` header. The server stores the key with the result; if a retry arrives with the same key, it returns the stored response instead of, say, charging a card twice. Payment APIs such as Stripe work this way.

**Avoiding lost updates.** Return an `ETag` with each resource. Clients send `If-Match: "v7"` with their PUT or PATCH, and the server answers `412 Precondition Failed` if someone else changed it in the meantime. This approach is called **optimistic concurrency**: assume no clash, but check.

**Rate limits.** Answer `429 Too Many Requests` with `Retry-After`, and document the limits. Clients should retry with **exponential backoff** (wait 1 s, then 2 s, 4 s...) plus a little random extra wait, called **jitter**, so many clients don't retry at the same instant.

**Slow jobs.** Answer `202 Accepted` with a URL the client can poll for progress.

**Versioning.** Avoid **breaking changes**, changes that make existing clients fail: adding fields is safe; removing or renaming them isn't. When a break is unavoidable, put a version in the path (`/v2/`) or in a header, run both versions for a while, and announce the old one's end with `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers.
concepts.code:
POST /v1/payments HTTP/1.1              # first try: the network drops the answer
Host: api.example.com
Content-Type: application/json
Idempotency-Key: 6f1c2a9e-3b7d-4e0f-9a55-2c8d1e7b4f10

{"amount": 1999, "currency": "EUR"}

POST /v1/payments HTTP/1.1              # retry with the SAME key
Host: api.example.com
Content-Type: application/json
Idempotency-Key: 6f1c2a9e-3b7d-4e0f-9a55-2c8d1e7b4f10

{"amount": 1999, "currency": "EUR"}

HTTP/1.1 201 Created                    # the stored result; no second charge
Content-Type: application/json

{"id": "pay_81", "status": "succeeded"}

HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests          # slow down...
Retry-After: 30                         # ...try again in 30 seconds
takeaways: Prefer cursor pagination for large or changing lists
An Idempotency-Key makes POST retries safe
If-Match + ETag prevents lost updates (412 on a clash)
429 + Retry-After; clients back off, with jitter
pitfalls: Making up a new idempotency key for each retry, which defeats its purpose.

quiz.q: Why does an idempotency key need to stay the same across retries?
options: The server recognises the retry by the key and returns the original result
It's used to scramble the body
quiz.explain: Only a repeated key lets the server detect a duplicate and avoid a second charge.

concepts.name: Inside TLS 1.3
concepts.summary: Walk through the TLS 1.3 handshake in detail: key exchange, SNI, ALPN, certificate chains, resumption, 0-RTT and forward secrecy.
concepts.why: Diagnosing handshake failures, certificate errors and connection delays at scale requires knowing what each message does.
concepts.body:
TLS relies on **public-key cryptography**: each side can have a key pair, a public key anyone may see and a private key kept secret. Data locked with one key can only be opened with the other, and a **digital signature** made with a private key can be checked by anyone holding the public key. A TLS 1.3 handshake fits in one round trip.

**ClientHello**, the client's first message, carries: the **cipher suites** it supports (named combinations of encryption methods, such as AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305); a **key share**, a single-use public key for agreeing on a secret (commonly X25519, increasingly paired with a newer method designed to resist future quantum computers); **SNI**, the hostname it wants, so one server can hold certificates for many sites; and ALPN, the HTTP versions it speaks.

**ServerHello** picks the options and sends the server's own key share. Both sides can now compute the same secret without it ever crossing the network, and everything after is encrypted: the server's **certificate chain**, a signature proving it holds the certificate's private key, and Finished messages that confirm neither side's messages were tampered with.

The client checks the chain: the site's own certificate, issued for this hostname; then intermediate certificates; up to a root certificate built into the device. Each must be within its dates and not withdrawn. Forgetting to send an intermediate is a classic mistake: some browsers have one remembered and work, others fail.

**Forward secrecy**: because key shares are used once and thrown away, someone who steals the server's private key later still can't decrypt traffic they recorded earlier.

**Resumption**: the server gives the client a session ticket; next time, the client uses it to skip the certificate work. With **0-RTT early data**, it can even send its first request immediately. But an attacker can capture and resend that early data, a **replay attack**, so servers should accept only safe, idempotent requests in it.

SNI is still sent unencrypted; **Encrypted Client Hello** (ECH) hides it, using keys published in DNS `HTTPS` records.
concepts.code:
# Show the agreed protocol, cipher suite, ALPN result and certificate check
$ openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com \
    -alpn h2,http/1.1 </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | grep -E "^(New|ALPN|Server Temp Key|Verify return)"
Server Temp Key: X25519, 253 bits             # the key exchange method
New, TLSv1.3, Cipher is TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384  # the cipher suite
ALPN protocol: h2                             # HTTP/2 was chosen
Verify return code: 0 (ok)                    # the certificate chain checked out

# Print each certificate in the chain the server sends (s: = subject, i: = issuer)
$ openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com -showcerts </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
    | grep -E "^ *[0-9] s:|i:"
takeaways: TLS 1.3 takes 1 round trip: ClientHello with key share, ServerHello, then encrypted certificate and Finished
SNI picks the certificate; ALPN picks h2 or http/1.1
Single-use key shares give forward secrecy
0-RTT data can be replayed: allow only idempotent requests
pitfalls: Sending only the site's own certificate without the intermediates, which fails on clients that haven't remembered them.

quiz.q: Why must servers be careful with 0-RTT early data?
options: It switches off forward secrecy for the whole session
An attacker can capture and resend it
quiz.explain: Early data has no protection against being resent, so a captured request could be replayed.

concepts.name: Advanced caching: Vary, keys and revalidation
concepts.summary: Master cache keys, Vary, stale-while-revalidate, stale-if-error, guessed freshness and strategies for replacing cached copies.
concepts.why: Subtle caching mistakes leak private data, keep old versions live after a release, or swamp your servers at the worst moment.
concepts.body:
A cache files each response under a **cache key**: by default the method and URL. `Vary` adds request headers to the key, so `Vary: Accept-Encoding` keeps the gzip and Brotli versions apart. `Vary: Cookie` or `Vary: User-Agent` make almost every request unique, so the share of requests answered from the cache, the **hit rate**, collapses. Instead, simplify at the CDN, for example by sorting browsers into just "mobile" and "desktop", or by using different URLs.

**Age and freshness.** A copy is fresh while its age is below its allowed lifetime: `s-maxage` for shared caches, otherwise `max-age`, otherwise `Expires`. With none of these, caches may make up a lifetime themselves, often 10% of the time since `Last-Modified`; this is **heuristic freshness**. That's why responses without explicit headers sometimes get cached unexpectedly: always send `Cache-Control`.

**Serving stale copies on purpose:**

- `stale-while-revalidate=60`: after expiry, keep serving the old copy for up to 60 s while fetching a fresh one in the background, so users never wait for the check.
- `stale-if-error=86400`: if the origin server fails, keep serving the old copy for a day.

**Request collapsing.** When a popular item expires, CDNs merge the many simultaneous requests for it into one request to the origin, protecting it from a stampede.

**Replacing cached copies**, best first:

- file names containing a content hash, with `immutable` (nothing ever needs replacing)
- short lifetimes plus `stale-while-revalidate`
- purging by tag: label responses with `Surrogate-Key` or `Cache-Tag` headers, then tell the CDN to drop everything with a tag when it changes
- purging single URLs

`Clear-Site-Data: "cache"` wipes a user's browser cache for your site, for example at logout.

`Cache-Control: private` responses can still sit in the browser cache on a shared computer; use `no-store` for truly sensitive pages.
concepts.code:
# A news article: browsers check each time; the CDN keeps it 5 minutes,
# serves the old copy while refreshing, and for a day if the origin is down
Cache-Control: public, max-age=0, s-maxage=300, stale-while-revalidate=60, stale-if-error=86400
ETag: "article-812-v14"
Vary: Accept-Encoding
Cache-Tag: article-812, section-tech      # CDN-specific: purge by tag on edit

# A file with a hash in its name: never checked, never purged
# /assets/app.3f9a1c.js
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

# Account page with personal data
Cache-Control: no-store

# Mistake: every different cookie value becomes a separate cached copy
Vary: Cookie
takeaways: Cache key = method + URL + the headers named in Vary; keep Vary short
Always send Cache-Control to avoid guessed lifetimes
stale-while-revalidate hides the check; stale-if-error survives outages
Prefer hashed file names and tag purges over purging URLs
pitfalls: Adding Vary: User-Agent and quietly dropping the CDN hit rate to almost zero.

quiz.q: A response has Last-Modified but no Cache-Control or Expires. What may a cache do?
options: Store it with a lifetime it works out itself
quiz.explain: RFC 9111 allows heuristic freshness, commonly a fraction of the time since Last-Modified.

concepts.name: Network performance end to end
concepts.summary: Reason about latency, bandwidth and round trips, and use connection reuse, compression, early hints, priorities and prefetching.
concepts.why: On real networks, round trips rather than raw speed decide load time, and fixes at the protocol level beat tweaking code.
concepts.body:
A connection has two kinds of speed: **bandwidth**, how much data it carries per second, and latency, how long each round trip takes. For most web pages latency dominates. A round trip costs tens of milliseconds on a good connection and hundreds on mobile or across continents, and a cold request pays for DNS, TCP and TLS before the request itself. Cut round trips first.

**Reuse connections and open them early.** Keep-alive and HTTP/2 or 3 reuse one connection. Avoid needless extra origins: each costs new handshakes. For other sites you do need, `<link rel="preconnect">` in the page's HTML does the DNS, TCP and TLS work early.

**Send less, sooner:**

- Compress text with Brotli or zstd (`Content-Encoding: br` or `zstd`).
- Use modern image formats, in sizes that fit the screen.
- TCP's slow start means a new connection can send only about 14 KB in its first round trip. So keep the start of the HTML small, and put the styles needed for the first screen directly into it.

**Use the server's thinking time.** While the server is still building a page, it can send `103 Early Hints` with `Link: </app.css>; rel=preload` headers, so the browser starts fetching important files during the wait. Sending the top of the HTML before the rest is ready has a similar effect.

**Priorities.** Over HTTP/2 and 3, browsers fetch styles and fonts before images; the `Priority` header and the `fetchpriority` attribute adjust this.

**Skip the request entirely**: long caching, prefetching pages the user will probably open next, and CDNs close to users.

Measure with data from real visitors, such as Google's Core Web Vitals: **TTFB** (time to first byte, how long until the response starts arriving) and LCP (how long until the main content is shown). The Network tab breaks each request into queueing, DNS, connecting, TLS, waiting (TTFB) and download.
concepts.code:
# Where does the time go? (each time includes the steps before it)
$ curl -so /dev/null -w "dns:%{time_namelookup} connect:%{time_connect} tls:%{time_appconnect} ttfb:%{time_starttransfer} total:%{time_total}\n" https://example.com
dns:0.004 connect:0.031 tls:0.068 ttfb:0.152 total:0.153

# Compression: compare the bytes actually downloaded
$ curl -so /dev/null -w "%{size_download}\n" https://example.com/app.js
$ curl -so /dev/null -w "%{size_download}\n" -H "Accept-Encoding: br" https://example.com/app.js

# 103 Early Hints, sent before the real response
HTTP/1.1 103 Early Hints
Link: </css/app.css>; rel=preload; as=style
Link: <https://cdn.example.com>; rel=preconnect

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
takeaways: Latency and round trips usually matter more than bandwidth
Reuse connections; preconnect to other sites you need
103 Early Hints uses the server's thinking time to start downloads
Measure TTFB and LCP from real visitors
pitfalls: Shaving bytes while the page still waits on several round trips, one after another, to different origins.

quiz.q: A page fetches a script from a new third-party origin discovered late. Which hint removes the most setup latency?
options: A larger TCP window on your own server
quiz.explain: preconnect finishes the DNS, TCP and TLS work before the script is even requested.
